title: Heaven’s Council and Satan’s Approach
setting: Heaven, then the outer shell of the World, the sun, and Mount Niphates above Eden
summary: After an invocation to Light, the poem moves to Heaven, where God foresees Satan’s success and Man’s fall, explains that Man was made free, and promises grace. The Son offers to die for Man and is exalted, and the angels sing. Meanwhile Satan lands on the bare outside of the World, finds the stairway to Heaven, flies to the sun, and tricks the archangel Uriel into pointing him to Paradise.

sections.title: Hail, holy Light
sections.note: Rising out of Hell and Chaos, the poet greets Light, then mourns his own blindness and asks to be given inward sight instead. It is the most personal passage in the poem.

sections.title: God looks down
sections.note: From his throne, with the Son at his right hand, God sees Adam and Eve in the garden and Satan approaching the World.

sections.title: God foretells the Fall
sections.note: God tells the Son that Man will fall, and insists the fault is Man’s own: he was made ‘sufficient to have stood, though free to fall.’ Because Man will be deceived rather than self-tempted, he will find grace.

sections.title: The Son pleads for Man
sections.note: The Son praises the promise of grace and asks whether God will really let Satan win, or unmake his own creation.

sections.title: God sets the terms
sections.note: God promises to renew Man’s powers and give him Conscience as a guide, but justice demands a death for Man’s treason. He asks who in Heaven will die to pay it.

sections.title: The Son offers himself
sections.note: Heaven falls silent; no angel volunteers. Then the Son offers his own life, foreseeing that he will rise, defeat Death, and bring the redeemed home.

sections.title: God exalts the Son
sections.note: God accepts, decrees that the Son will be born as a man, and names him universal King, ‘by merit more than birthright Son of God.’ He foretells the Last Judgement and a new Heaven and Earth.

sections.title: The angels’ hymn
sections.note: The angels cast down their crowns of amaranth and sing to the Father, too bright to be seen, and to the Son, through whom he is seen.

sections.title: Satan on the outer shell; the Paradise of Fools
sections.note: Satan walks the dark, windy outer surface of the World like a vulture on a plain. The narrator imagines this place as the future limbo of vanity, and turns it into satire on monks, pilgrims and relics.

sections.title: The stairway to Heaven
sections.note: Satan finds a golden stairway like Jacob’s ladder and an opening down into the World. From its lowest step he takes in the whole universe at once, with wonder and with envy.

sections.title: Satan flies to the sun
sections.note: Satan plunges among the stars and lands on the sun, a place of light brighter than any metal or jewel. The narrator compares it to the alchemists’ dream of the philosopher’s stone.

sections.title: Uriel, and Satan’s disguise
sections.note: Satan sees a glorious angel standing in the sun and disguises himself as a young cherub. The angel turns: it is Uriel, one of the seven who stand nearest God’s throne.

sections.title: Satan deceives Uriel
sections.note: Posing as an eager admirer of God’s works, Satan asks where Man lives. Hypocrisy is invisible to all but God, so Uriel describes the creation and points out Paradise, and Satan lands on Mount Niphates.

glosses.note: Uncreated, existing from eternity.
A Latin idiom: ‘would you rather be called.’ Milton is trying out names for Light.
Orpheus, the legendary singer who went down to the underworld; a hymn to Night was attributed to him.
A translation of gutta serena, the medical term for the kind of blindness Milton had; ‘suffusion’ in line 26 is a cataract.
A Thracian poet blinded for challenging the Muses. Maeonides is Homer; Tiresias and Phineus were blind prophets.
In the dark. The ‘wakeful bird’ is the nightingale.
Flattering, smoothly deceptive.
Consigned to destruction, doomed.
In spite of.
Delight, the one in whom I am pleased.
Amaranth, from the Greek for ‘unfading,’ a flower that never wilts.
Opaque, dark.
A mountain range of central Asia, roughly the Himalaya and Hindu Kush.
China. Travellers reported that the Chinese drove light wagons fitted with sails.
A Greek philosopher said to have leapt into Etna so that people would think he had become a god.
A young man who drowned himself after reading Plato’s dialogue on the immortality of the soul.
Carmelite, Dominican and Franciscan friars, named by the colour of their habits.
A supposed wobble in the heavens, explained in old astronomy by a ninth, crystalline sphere; the ‘first moved’ is the outermost sphere, the Primum Mobile.
Aries, the Ram, which seems to carry Andromeda. From Libra to Aries is half the zodiac.
The telescope; Galileo had recently observed spots on the sun.
Mercury, or quicksilver, which alchemists tried to fix; Proteus, the shape-changing sea god, stands for matter in its changing forms.
Alembic, a still used in distilling.
The sun as master alchemist, believed to ripen metals and jewels underground.
In Revelation 19, John sees ‘an angel standing in the sun.’
Tucked up, girded for speed.
Hebrew for ‘light of God,’ one of the seven archangels of Jewish tradition who stand before God’s throne.
Three-formed: the moon waxing, full and waning, and the triple goddess of the moon, Diana and Hecate.
A mountain in Armenia, near the region where Eden was placed.

famous.why: ‘Hail, holy Light’ opens the poem’s most celebrated invocation, wrestling with how to name light without error.
Milton’s lament for his blindness, ‘Thus with the year seasons return; but not to me returns day,’ is among the most moving lines in English.
‘Sufficient to have stood, though free to fall’ is the poem’s central statement on free will.
The Son’s ‘Behold me then: me for him, life for life I offer’ answers Satan’s lone volunteering in Book 2 with its opposite.
‘Dark with excessive bright thy skirts appear’ finds a paradox for God to match Hell’s ‘darkness visible.’
Hypocrisy as ‘the only evil that walks invisible, except to God alone’ excuses Uriel and warns the reader.

themes: Free will is the hinge of the poem: God foresees the Fall but does not cause it.
Mercy answers justice, and the Son’s free self-offering mirrors and reverses Satan’s pride.
Light, physical and spiritual, runs through the book, from Milton’s blindness to the blaze of the sun.
Evil can pass for good: Satan’s first success is a lie told to an honest angel.
art: Satan, disguised as a young cherub with a silver wand, approaching the radiant archangel Uriel as he stands in the blazing disc of the sun.
